title: Host-offload activation & PCIe-aware shard rebalancing notes
body:
Purpose
This note collects a practical design for reducing peak GPU memory pressure during multi-GPU inference by offloading activation buffers to host pinned memory and coupling that with a PCIe/NVLink-aware shard rebalancing strategy for the KV cache. The goal is to increase effective batch capacity and lower OOM risk while keeping tail latency within SLOs.

Context and motivation
- We routinely see variance in activation footprint across request types (long prompts, long generation). Dedicated slots tuned for median footprint still hit OOM for outliers or bursty traffic.
- Current designs assume KV shards live entirely on-device and rely on NCCL collectives for inter-GPU exchange. That is efficient when NVLink is available and memory headroom exists, but brittle when host memory is underutilized or when GPUs are heterogeneous or connected only via PCIe.
- Offloading activations to host memory can buy headroom for KV shards and model weights, but naive offload is expensive for latency-critical paths. We need a plan that is adaptive and PCIe-topology-aware.

Constraints and failure modes
- PCIe transfer bandwidth and latency are much worse than NVLink/GDR, so frequent round-trips will break tail latency.
- Host pinned allocations must be stable and reclaimed carefully; page faults are catastrophic for latency.
- When offloading activations, we must maintain correct KV lifetimes and attention cache coherence across shards during generation.
- Rebalancing KV shards (moving ownership between GPUs) risks transient performance regressions and must be incremental and reversible.

Design overview
1) Two-tier activation residency
   - Fast-resident buffer: small on-GPU circular buffer kept for the most recent tokens (configurable, e.g., last 32 tokens). This is used for immediate decoding and kernel fusion.
   - Staged host-resident archive: older activations moved to host pinned memory, optionally compressed. Moves are asynchronous and prefetching happens when the decoder anticipates needing older prefixes (heuristic described below).

2) Asynchronous PCIe transfer pipeline
   - Use cudaMemcpyAsync to/from pinned host buffers and CUDA streams dedicated per GPU to avoid interference with compute streams.
   - Prioritize transfers on dedicated NIC/CPU cores when GPUDirect is available for RDMA-enabled fabrics; fall back to host copies otherwise.
   - Transfer batching: coalesce small activation pages into larger contiguous pinned segments to amortize PCIe cost. Chunk size heuristic tuned by median sequence-length * hidden-size.

3) Lightweight activation compression
   - Quantize archived activations to fp16 or int8 (symmetric) before transfer; provide LZ4 fallback for rare large compressibility cases. Quantization helps reduce PCIe footprint with minimal compute overhead on CPU/GPU.

4) PCIe/NVLink topology-aware KV shard placement and rebalancing
   - Topology oracle: detect per-host NVLink groups, PCIe root complexes, and device-peer bandwidth matrix at startup.
   - Prefer placing hot KV shards (higher access frequency based on recent traffic) on GPUs that are within NVLink domain of the decoding GPU(s). Cold shards can be placed on GPUs connected over PCIe or even entirely off-GPU on host-resident accelerated stores.
   - Rebalance policy: continuous background profiler tracks access rates at shard granularity; when imbalance exceeds thresholds (e.g., 2x stddev across GPUs) trigger incremental migrations. Migrations are per-microshard (sub-shard grain) to reduce transient load.

5) Lazy materialization and prefetch hints
   - Instead of eagerly copying an entire offloaded activation region back for each new token, materialize only the minimal KV slices needed for the next N tokens.
   - Use decoder-side heuristics (next-token entropy, beam size, current generation length) to estimate lookahead and prefetch accordingly.

6) NCCL tuning knobs and fallback rules
   - When NVLink connectivity forms a contiguous group, use NCCL ring collectives for reduce-scatter/all-gather with tuned chunk sizes (empirically derived).
   - For PCIe-only paths or cross-host exchanges where NVLink is absent or uneven, fall back to pairwise asynchronous point-to-point copies and schedule communications on dedicated streams; disable large NCCL multicast which penalizes PCIe topologies.

Operational heuristics and safety
- Graceful degradation: if PCIe transfer latency increases beyond threshold, system automatically expands fast-resident buffer size (shrink host-offload) to avoid stalls for ongoing generations.
- Migration backpressure: background rebalancer monitors GPU utilization; if migrations would push utilization above margin, pause migrations and queue until headroom frees.
- Canary mode: enable host-offload per-pool via runtime flag. Start with pools for lower-SLA workloads and gradually roll to higher-SLA after validation.

Metrics and experiments to run
- Memory headroom increase: measure average and p95 GPU free memory per slot before/after offload. Target: >20% increase without significantly increasing tail latency.
- Latency impact: end-to-end generation p50/p95/p99 under mixed batch sizes. Target: p99 increase < 10% for median cases; identify patterns when p99 spikes occur.
- PCIe cost vs benefit: bytes moved to host per generated token and CPU utilization for compression.
- Migration overhead: measure throughput drop during shard rebalances and tune microshard size to limit impact to <5% throughput dip.

Implementation plan and milestones
1) Prototype: implement host pinned archive and simple async transfer pipeline with fp16 quantization for activations on a single-node multi-GPU setup. (owner: Lin)
2) Topology detection module: cross-host NVLink/PCIe matrix and simple placement API. (owner: Diego)
3) Background profiler and microshard migration engine; metrics + pause/resume control. (owner: Ravi)
4) NCCL fallback rules and per-topology collective selection logic. (owner: Aisha)
5) End-to-end integration test, canary rollout to dedicated pools, and synthetic benchmark suite.

Open questions and risks
- Compression tradeoffs: where does CPU cost for compression outweigh PCIe saving? Need microbenchmarks across our instance types.
- Debugging complexity: adding host residency and dynamic migrations increases operational surface and observability requirements. We need binary traces for activation lifetimes and transfer events.
- Consistency and correctness: ensure attention cache invariants when microshard migrations overlap with decoding; may need temporary replication for hot epochs.

Next actions
- Run a microbenchmark: measure cudaMemcpyAsync pinned-host <-> device throughput with concurrent compute on our representative instance types (A100, H100, L40x). Attach results to PR #1832.
- Sketch prefetch heuristics for decoder lookahead (simple model: prefetch when remaining-gen-length > fast-resident-size).
- Build minimal telemetry for offload transfers (timestamps, sizes, queue lengths).

Notes for reviewers
This is a high-level playbook; the intent is to provide a pragmatic path to reclaim GPU memory without wholesale redesign of the runtime. The real gains will depend on workload characteristics (prefix-heavy vs streaming) and our server topologies. Feedback welcome on shard granularity, compression defaults, and safe rollout thresholds.
